(CNN)  -- Over 28,000 Liverpool fans marked the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster in a special memorial service at Anfield on Wednesday. Liverpool supporters at the Kop end paid their respects in an emotional afternoon at Anfield. A total of 96 supporters died on April 15, 1989 before the FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday's stadium, the worst-ever tragedy in English sporting history. To commemorate the anniversary, the city of Liverpool came to a standstill at 3.06 pm (1406 GMT) with the bells of the two cathedrals and its civic buildings ringing out in memory of those fans who lost their lives. On Anfield's famous Kop, 96 candles were lit while commemorations took place at Hillsborough and also in Nottingham. Members of the current Liverpool team stood somberly as hymns were played before a roll call of the dead was read out. Club legend Kenny Dalglish, who was Liverpool manager at the time of the disaster, then read a short prayer. The mayor of Liverpool, Steve Rotherham, who was at the game 20 years ago, helped organize the emotional memorial. "Hillsborough affected so many lives, not just on Merseyside but across the whole of the UK," he said. "I attended the match 20 years ago and the passing years do not diminish the importance and the poignancy of this occasion." Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard, whose 10-year-old cousin Jon-Paul Gilhooley was the youngest victim of the tragedy, spoke of his feelings this week. "Time has gone by, but the scars will never ever be healed and the fans will never ever forget. So you can always rely on our supporters to be there for you when you need them." The Liverpool fans died in a crush which started just before the kick-off as the gate at the Leppings Lane End was opened with terrible consequences. The match started but when the scale of the tragedy became clear, it was swiftly abandoned at 3.06 pm. In the immediate aftermath, the British government commissioned Lord Justice Taylor to conduct an inquiry which would have a far-reaching impact on football. Taylor was deeply critical of the police operation at Hillsborough, but his most significant recommendations were the removal of perimeter fencing and the creation of all-seater stadia. His report also cleared Liverpool fans of blame for the tragedy after lurid tabloid headlines provoked revulsion on Merseyside. Prime minister Gordon Brown paid reference to the controversy in an interview released on Liverpool's official television channel. "It was wrong for people to blame, as some did, Liverpool fans on that day," he said. "That's probably what matters most -- that people understood that the behavior of Liverpool fans in helping each other was magnificent. "Let's never forget the fans who cruelly lost their lives on a day when we know the people of Liverpool were trying to help each other," he added. However, the people of Liverpool are still angry and bitter at the lack of justice for those who died -- and that frustration surfaced when Andy Burnham, the   Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport took to the stand to address the crowd. As Burnham spoke, the crowd rose as one to sing "Justice for the 96". The Kop chant boomed around the stadium and Burnham, an Everton fan, was left in no doubt about the strength of feeling over the lack of accountability from officialdom over the tragedy. Fittingly, the ceremony was concluded with Gerry Marsden leading the fans in singing Liverpool anthem 'You'll Never Walk Alone'.

## What Happened on 15 April 1989

The Hillsborough disaster occurred on 15 April 1989 at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield, England, during an FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. It remains the deadliest stadium-related disaster in British sporting history, claiming 97 lives.

The tragedy unfolded in the Leppings Lane end of the stadium, which was allocated to Liverpool supporters. As kick-off approached, a large crowd of fans gathered outside the turnstiles. To relieve the crush building outside, police match commander Chief Superintendent David Duckenfield ordered exit gate C to be opened.

This allowed a surge of supporters to enter through a tunnel leading directly into already-overcrowded central pens (pens 3 and 4). With no effective mechanism to direct fans to less crowded areas, the influx created a lethal crush against the perimeter fencing—fencing that had been installed to prevent pitch invasions during that era of hooliganism concerns.

Supporters were pressed against the barriers and each other, unable to escape. Many died of compressive asphyxia while standing. The match was stopped after six minutes as the scale of the emergency became apparent. Fans tore up advertising hoardings to use as makeshift stretchers.

## The Aftermath and the Long Fight for Truth

### Initial False Narratives

In the immediate aftermath, victims and Liverpool supporters were wrongly blamed. Some media outlets—most notoriously *The Sun* newspaper, under the headline "THE TRUTH"—published false allegations that drunken, ticketless fans had caused the disaster and that supporters had robbed and urinated on the dead. These claims were later comprehensively disproven, but they caused enduring pain to bereaved families and led to a decades-long boycott of *The Sun* across Merseyside.

### The Taylor Report

Lord Justice Peter Taylor was appointed to lead an official inquiry. His interim report was published in August 1989, with the final report following in January 1990.

The Taylor Report reached crucial conclusions:

- **The main cause** of the disaster was a failure of police crowd control. The report was explicit that the behaviour of fans was not to blame.
- It criticized the decision-making of senior officers on the day.
- It found the stadium's safety provisions and the physical layout—particularly the pens and perimeter fencing—to be dangerous.

The report's recommendations transformed British football. Its most significant legacy was the requirement that all top-flight and second-tier stadiums become **all-seater venues**, eliminating standing terraces. Perimeter fences were removed. These changes reshaped the matchday experience across English football and are credited with dramatically improving stadium safety.

### The Continuing Struggle

Despite the Taylor Report's findings, the original 1991 inquest returned verdicts of "accidental death," and the fight for full accountability continued for decades. The Hillsborough Independent Panel, reporting in 2012, revealed that police statements had been altered and that a coordinated effort had been made to deflect blame onto supporters. Fresh inquests concluded in 2016 that the 96 victims (at the time; a 97th death was later attributed to the disaster in 2021) had been **unlawfully killed**, and that supporters bore no responsibility.

## The 20th Anniversary Memorial at Anfield

On 15 April 2009, Liverpool marked the 20th anniversary of the disaster with a memorial service at Anfield, the club's home stadium. It became one of the most emotionally significant gatherings in the club's history.

An estimated **30,000 to 40,000 people** attended, far exceeding expectations and filling the stadium. Mourners included bereaved families, survivors, players past and present, and supporters not only of Liverpool but of Everton and other clubs, reflecting the broad solidarity the tragedy had inspired.

The service featured:

- The traditional singing of "You'll Never Walk Alone," the anthem forever associated with the club and the disaster.
- The reading of the names of all 96 who had died.
- A period of reflection at 3:06 pm, marking the moment the fateful match had been stopped.

A defining moment came when Andy Burnham, then the government's Culture Secretary, addressed the crowd. His speech was interrupted by chants of **"Justice for the 96"** from the assembled supporters—a powerful expression of the families' unresolved grievances and their continued demand for truth. This moment is widely credited with adding political momentum that contributed to the establishment of the Hillsborough Independent Panel later that year, which ultimately helped uncover the full truth.

## A Lasting Legacy

The Hillsborough disaster stands as a watershed in British football and public safety. It led directly to the modernization of stadiums nationwide, exposed institutional failures and cover-ups, and demonstrated the extraordinary determination of families who refused to accept a false narrative. The memory of the 97 continues to be honoured, and the phrase "You'll Never Walk Alone" remains an enduring symbol of that solidarity and remembrance.

---

*Note: The death toll is now recorded as 97, following the 2021 ruling regarding Andrew Devine, who died from injuries sustained in the disaster. Contemporary references to the 2009 memorial and earlier events typically cite 96 victims, the figure known at that time.*

# Thousands Gather at Anfield to Mark 20th Anniversary of Hillsborough Disaster

**LIVERPOOL** — A sea of red and white filled Anfield stadium today as an estimated 30,000 people gathered to remember the 96 Liverpool supporters who died in the Hillsborough disaster two decades ago, in a service marked by raw emotion, defiant calls for justice, and the enduring solidarity of a grieving city.

The memorial service, held on the pitch where the club has honored its dead for twenty years, brought together bereaved families, survivors, former players, and dignitaries to mark the tragedy that unfolded at Sheffield Wednesday's ground on April 15, 1989, during an FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest.

## Calls for Justice

The ceremony took an unexpectedly charged turn when chants of "Justice for the 96" erupted from the stands, underscoring the families' long-running grievance that no one has been held accountable for the crush that claimed so many lives. The spontaneous outpouring reflected two decades of frustration over what campaigners have long described as an incomplete accounting of that day's events.

The intensity of the moment served as a reminder that, for many families, the anniversary was not simply about mourning but about an ongoing fight for truth and accountability.

## A City United in Song

As the names of all 96 victims were read aloud, emotions swelled throughout the stadium. The service reached its most poignant moment with the singing of "You'll Never Walk Alone," the Liverpool anthem that has become inextricably linked with the disaster and its aftermath. Voices cracked and tears flowed as the crowd united in the song that has come to symbolize both the club's identity and the community's shared grief.

Ninety-six red balloons and a period of silence added to the solemnity of an occasion that blended sorrow with an unmistakable sense of collective strength.

## Players and Politicians Pay Tribute

Former players and club figures were among those who attended to pay their respects, standing alongside the families who have kept the memory of the 96 alive across two decades. Their presence reinforced the bond between the club and the supporters who lost their lives following the team they loved.

Political figures also attended and offered words of remembrance, acknowledging both the scale of the tragedy and the dignity with which the families have conducted their long campaign. The presence of public officials, however, was met with mixed feelings from some in the crowd, who continued to press for greater transparency.

## An Enduring Legacy

Twenty years on, the Hillsborough disaster remains one of the darkest chapters in British sporting history and a defining event for the city of Liverpool. Today's ceremony demonstrated that the passage of time has done little to dim either the pain of loss or the determination of a community that continues to say, together, that its dead will never walk alone.

---

*The 96 who died at Hillsborough are remembered each year at Anfield in a service that has become a fixture of the club's calendar and a testament to a city's unyielding solidarity.*
